# hexmap <a href="https://pkg.mitchelloharawild.com/hexmap/"><img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="138" alt="hexmap website" /></a>

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/mitchelloharawild/hexmap/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/mitchelloharawild/hexmap/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/hexmap)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=hexmap)
<!-- badges: end -->

hexmap converts a map of regions into a map of equally sized hexagons, one for each region. Every region gets the same amount of ink, so small but important regions (such as inner-city electorates) are as visible as large, sparsely populated ones, while each region stays close to where it is on the map.

## Installation

Install the development version from GitHub with:

``` r
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("mitchelloharawild/hexmap")
```

## Usage

`hexmap()` replaces each region of an `sf` object with a hexagon, keeping every other column and the order of the rows. Regions are placed to keep their relative positions, and distant islands such as Tasmania are tiled separately.

```{r usage, message = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "70%"}
library(hexmap)
hex <- hexmap(aus_election_2025)
hex
plot(hex["state"])
```

Use `group` to keep the hexagons of each group, such as a state, together and touching the same neighbouring groups as on the map:

```{r usage-group, message = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "70%"}
hex <- hexmap(aus_election_2025, group = state)
plot(hex["state"])
```

Use `layout` to choose how the groups are arranged. See [`vignette("layouts")`](https://pkg.mitchelloharawild.com/hexmap/articles/layouts.html) for how the layouts compare.

```{r usage-layout, message = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "70%"}
hex <- hexmap(aus_election_2025, group = state, layout = layout_compact())
plot(hex["state"])
```

The hexagons are regular in the projection they are made in, which is an equal-area projection for longitude/latitude maps unless you choose one with `crs`. See [`vignette("projections")`](https://pkg.mitchelloharawild.com/hexmap/articles/projections.html).

```{r usage-crs, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "70%"}
hex <- hexmap(aus_election_2025, group = state, crs = 3577)
plot(hex["state"])
```

Given a geometry column, `hexmap()` returns a geometry column of hexagons, so you can keep both:

```{r usage-column, message = FALSE}
aus_election_2025 |>
  dplyr::mutate(hex = hexmap(geometry, group = state))
```

## Example: the 2025 Australian federal election

Labor won 94 of the 150 seats at the 2025 Australian federal election. On a geographic map the result looks like a Coalition win, as the large rural divisions hide Labor's many small city seats. A cartogram produced with [cartogram](https://github.com/sjewo/cartogram), which distorts regions so their areas are proportional to a variable, can give each division an equal area to show the number of seats, but it distorts the map beyond recognition. A hexagon grid produced with [geogrid](https://github.com/jbaileyh/geogrid), which allocates regions to a regular grid of hexagons or squares, gives each division the same space, but doesn't keep states together. hexmap keeps each state together, in its place and with its neighbours.

```{r election-setup, include = FALSE, ref.label = "election-data"}
```

```{r animation, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6.5, dpi = 100, fig.show = "animate", animation.hook = "gifski", interval = 1/20}
library(ggplot2)

colours <- c(Labor = "#D7263D", Coalition = "#1F4E9C", Greens = "#2E9E44", Other = "#8C8C8C")
election_hexmap <- hexmap(election, group = state)

# Resample a closed ring to n points equally spaced along its boundary, anticlockwise
resample_ring <- function(xy, n = 60) {
  if (sum(xy[-1, 1] * xy[-nrow(xy), 2] - xy[-nrow(xy), 1] * xy[-1, 2]) < 0) xy <- xy[nrow(xy):1, ]
  s <- c(0, cumsum(sqrt(rowSums(diff(xy)^2))))
  at <- seq(0, max(s), length.out = n + 1)[-(n + 1)]
  cbind(approx(s, xy[, 1], at, ties = mean)$y, approx(s, xy[, 2], at, ties = mean)$y)
}

# Pair the outer ring of each part of each region with its hexagon, starting
# the hexagon at the point that best matches the ring
morph_rings <- function(from, to, n = 60) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(from), function(i) {
    hex <- resample_ring(st_coordinates(to[[i]])[, 1:2], n)
    parts <- lapply(unclass(st_cast(from[i], "POLYGON")), function(p) p[[1]])
    do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(parts), function(j) {
      ring <- resample_ring(parts[[j]], n)
      cost <- sapply(0:(n - 1), function(k) sum((ring - hex[(seq_len(n) + k - 1) %% n + 1, ])^2))
      hex <- hex[(seq_len(n) + which.min(cost) - 2) %% n + 1, ]
      data.frame(region = i, ring = paste(i, j),
                 x0 = ring[, 1], y0 = ring[, 2], x1 = hex[, 1], y1 = hex[, 2])
    }))
  }))
}

rings <- morph_rings(st_geometry(election), st_geometry(election_hexmap))
rings$party <- election$party[rings$region]

# Pause on the map, ease into the hexagons, pause, then ease back
ease <- c(rep(0, 10), (1 - cos(pi * seq(0, 1, length.out = 30))) / 2, rep(1, 15))
for (t in c(ease, rev(ease))) {
  frame <- transform(rings, x = x0 + t * (x1 - x0), y = y0 + t * (y1 - y0))
  print(
    ggplot(frame, aes(x, y, group = ring, fill = party)) +
      geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = colours, breaks = names(colours), name = NULL) +
      coord_equal(xlim = range(rings$x0, rings$x1), ylim = range(rings$y0, rings$y1)) +
      theme_void() +
      theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  )
}
```

The results are included as `aus_election_2025`: the simplified boundaries of each division from the [Australian Bureau of Statistics](https://www.abs.gov.au/), with its state and winning party from the [Australian Electoral Commission](https://www.aec.gov.au/) (CC BY 4.0). The maps below use the Australian Albers equal-area projection, with minor parties combined:

```{r election-data, message = FALSE}
library(sf)
library(hexmap)

party <- c(ALP = "Labor", LP = "Coalition", LNP = "Coalition", NP = "Coalition",
           GRN = "Greens")
election <- st_transform(aus_election_2025, 3577)
election$party <- ifelse(election$party %in% names(party), party[election$party], "Other")
```

Each method gives every division the same area:

```{r election-maps, message = FALSE}
library(cartogram)
library(geogrid)

# Cartogram
election$seats <- 1
election_cartogram <- cartogram_cont(election, "seats", itermax = 20)

# geogrid
grid <- calculate_grid(election, grid_type = "hexagonal", seed = 1)
election_geogrid <- assign_polygons(election, grid)

# hexmap
election_hexmap <- hexmap(election, group = state)
```

```{r comparison, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7}
library(patchwork)

election_map <- function(map, title) {
  # Merge each state's regions, closing small gaps between them
  d <- 0.03 * sqrt(median(as.numeric(st_area(map))))
  states <- aggregate(st_buffer(map["state"], d), list(map$state), length)
  states <- st_buffer(st_buffer(states, -d), 0)
  ggplot(map) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = party), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
    geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.3) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colours, breaks = names(colours), name = NULL) +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void()
}

election_map(election, "Geographic map") +
  election_map(election_cartogram, "Cartogram") +
  election_map(election_geogrid, "geogrid") +
  election_map(election_hexmap, "hexmap, grouped by state") +
  plot_layout(nrow = 2, guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Colouring the divisions by state shows the difference: geogrid scatters each state's divisions across the grid, putting four of Tasmania's five seats on the mainland, while hexmap keeps each state in one piece, touching the same states as on the map.

```{r states, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.5}
state_map <- function(map, title) {
  ggplot(map) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = state), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = unname(palette.colors(8, "Set 2")), name = NULL) +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void()
}

state_map(election_geogrid, "geogrid") +
  state_map(election_hexmap, "hexmap, grouped by state") +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```
